newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso gets another re-election boost.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso gets another re-election boost.

text.p: Fernando Henrique Cardoso's plan to become Brazil's first president who can seek a second term got another boost on Wednesday when the lower house of Congress rejected changes to a bill allowing re-election.

Outnumbered opposition lawmakers failed to muster enough votes in the Chamber of Deputies to approve amendments calling for a referendum on re-election and forcing Cardoso to stand down if he is allowed to seek a second term in 1998.
"Without a doubt another success," Jose Anibal, chief whip of Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB), said.

Cardoso scored the biggest victory of his two-year term on Tuesday when the lower house approved a constitutional amendment allowing sitting presidents, state governors and mayors the chance to run for a second term.

Although the bill still faces a second vote in the lower house and two in the Senate, each requiring 60 percent majorities, political commentators said the president's re-election dream had overcome its biggest hurdle.

"Cardoso succeeded in passing the first and most difficult test. It was a significant victory for the government, which expects the passage of the bill through its next stages to be more tranquil," financial daily Gazeta Mercantil said.
Cardoso himself kept a low profile, declining to join in the euphoria with which his supporters greeted Tuesday's vote.

"Congress has shown once again that it can express what the country wants," the president said during a ceremony. "We will continue to work, humbly and without arrogance ... for (re-election) to be approved a second time and in the Senate."
Brazil has banned re-election since the founding of the republic because of fears of a revival of imperial power.

But Cardoso argues the economic reforms he launched as finance minister in 1994, which have brought inflation down from 5,000 percent a year to just 10 percent in 1996, need political continuity to prosper. He hopes to emulate presidents Carlos Menem of Argentina and Alberto Fujimori of Peru, both of whom rewrote their countries' constitutions to allow their re-elections.

Business leaders, who back the Brazilian government's newfound enthusiasm for fiscal prudence and privatisation, said Cardoso's re-election would represent another step away from the economic chaos that engulfed the country for decades.
"A second Cardoso term means that for the first time in our lives we will be able to plan for the real long-term," said Luiz Fernando Furlan, president of meat processing giant Sadia.
The prospect of four more years on top of the two still left in his current term is widely seen as bolstering Cardoso's prestige in Brazil's notoriously unruly Congress.

But analysts were sceptical about his chances of racing ahead with reforms of the civil service, taxes and pensions, considered keys to the long-term success of his economic programme, which have been on hold for the re-election debate.
"Cardoso will definitely have some momentum now but how much? This is not going to solve all the reform problems," Gene Frieda, a New York-based consultant, said.
